questions.question: can I get a fee waiver for naturalization?
questions.answer:
The Application for Naturalization (Form N-400) is listed as a form eligible for a general fee waiver for requestors who demonstrate an inability to pay [S3]. However, eligibility requirements have varied over time and may not be current:

*   As of October 2019, USCIS restricted fee waivers to those with documented annual household income at or below 150% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines (FPG) or those who can establish financial hardship [S5].
*   Under a 2020 rule, fee waivers were permitted only if the applicant’s annual gross household income was 125% or less of the FPG and the applicant submitted the required USCIS form and accompanying documents [S2].

Because these sources describe past regulations, they may not reflect current eligibility criteria.

questions.question: I have a disability and cannot learn English. Is there an exception to the English test?
questions.answer: Yes, an exception to the English and civics requirements is available for applicants who are unable to comply due to a "medically determinable" physical or developmental disability or mental impairment that has lasted, or is expected to last, at least 12 months [S1]. The applicant must demonstrate that the disability or impairment affects their functioning such that they cannot meet the requirements, even with reasonable accommodations [S1]. To request this exception, a licensed medical professional must complete Form N-648, Medical Certification for Disability Exceptions, and certify that the disability prevents the applicant from meeting the English requirement, the civics requirement, or both [S1]. This exception is distinct from a "reasonable accommodation," which modifies the manner in which an applicant takes the test but does not exempt them from the requirements [S3][S4].

questions.question: I am 68 and have had a green card for 22 years. Do I still have to take the English test?
questions.answer: An alien is exempt from the English language requirement if they are age 55 or older and have lived as a lawful permanent resident (LPR) in the United States for at least 15 years [S2]. Additionally, an alien who is 65 or older and has resided in the United States as an LPR for at least 20 years is exempt from the English requirement [S3].

questions.question: I was outside the United States for eight months. Does that break my continuous residence?
questions.answer: An absence of more than 6 months but less than 1 year is presumed to break the continuity of residence [S1][S2]. Because an 8-month absence falls within this timeframe, it is presumed to break your continuous residence [S2][S4]. However, this presumption is rebuttable, meaning you may provide evidence to establish that you did not disrupt your residence [S2][S4]. Such evidence may include documentation that you did not terminate your U.S. employment, your immediate family remained in the United States, or you retained access to a home in the United States [S2].

questions.question: USCIS interviewed me over a year ago and still has not decided my case. What can I do?
questions.answer: USCIS is required to issue a decision on a naturalization application within 120 days of the initial interview [S1]. If USCIS fails to make a determination within this 120-day period, an applicant may apply to the United States district court for the district in which they reside for a hearing on the matter [S1][S2][S4]. The district court has jurisdiction to either determine the application itself or remand the matter to USCIS with instructions [S2][S4].

questions.question: My naturalization application was denied. Can I appeal it?
questions.answer: If a naturalization application is denied, an applicant may request a hearing before an immigration officer, which constitutes an administrative appeal [S4]. Once administrative remedies are exhausted, an applicant may seek judicial review of the denial in a United States district court under 8 U.S.C. § 1421(c) [S2][S3][S5]. Additionally, 28 U.S.C. § 1361 provides a potential avenue for relief for the failure to perform a clear, nondiscretionary duty, though this is considered an extraordinary remedy [S5].

questions.question: How long do I have to be married to a U.S. citizen before I can apply for citizenship?
questions.answer:
The provided sources do not specify a minimum duration for the marriage contract itself for all applicants. However, they do outline the following time requirements for your relationship:

*   **For spouses residing in the United States:** You must have been "living in marital union" with your U.S. citizen spouse for at least 3 years immediately preceding the filing of your application [S1][S2][S4]. During those 3 years, your spouse must have been a U.S. citizen [S2].
*   **For spouses of U.S. citizens regularly stationed abroad in qualifying employment:** You must have been married to the citizen spouse for at least one year [S5].

questions.question: I gave a wrong answer at my interview. Can that count against my good moral character?
questions.answer: Giving false testimony for the purpose of obtaining immigration or naturalization benefits precludes a finding of good moral character [S4][S5]. To qualify as false testimony that prevents a finding of good moral character, the statement must be an oral statement made under oath with the subjective intent of obtaining immigration or naturalization benefits [S4]. This rule applies even if the misrepresentation is not material [S4]. More broadly, good moral character is evaluated on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the standards of the average citizen in the community of residence [S1][S3].

questions.question: Can I still naturalize if I am in removal proceedings?
questions.answer:
Except for certain applications based on military service, USCIS lacks the authority to grant naturalization if there is a pending removal proceeding initiated by a warrant of arrest, and officers are instructed to deny such applications [S1]. An NTA is considered a warrant of arrest for this purpose, except in the 9th Circuit [S1]. Administrative closure of removal proceedings does not terminate them [S1].

Federal courts disagree on whether a district court may grant relief while removal proceedings are pending [S2][S3]. The majority of circuits (including the 2nd, 5th, 6th, 9th, and 10th) hold that § 1429 bars federal consideration of naturalization petitions during pending removal proceedings [S2][S3]. However, the 3rd and 7th Circuits have held that while a district court cannot order the Attorney General to naturalize an individual in these circumstances, it may grant declaratory relief by declaring the individual eligible for naturalization [S3].

questions.question: Will two DUI convictions stop me from becoming a citizen?
questions.answer: Evidence of two or more DUI convictions during the statutory period establishes a rebuttable presumption that an applicant lacks good moral character [S1]. This presumption may be overcome if the applicant provides substantial, relevant, and credible evidence that they possessed good moral character during the period in which the offenses were committed and that the convictions were an aberration [S1]. Efforts to reform or rehabilitate after multiple DUI convictions do not, in and of themselves, demonstrate good moral character during the period that includes the convictions [S1].

questions.question: If I sue because USCIS never decided, can the judge grant my citizenship, or does it go back to USCIS?
questions.answer: If a district court intervenes under 8 U.S.C. § 1447(b) because USCIS failed to make a determination within 120 days, the court has the authority to either determine the matter itself or remand the matter to USCIS with instructions to determine it [S2][S5]. Even if the court determines the matter in the applicant's favor, USCIS retains the "sole authority" to naturalize the applicant, which includes the final steps of administering the oath of allegiance and issuing the certificate of naturalization [S5].

questions.question: Is a notice to appear the same thing as a warrant of arrest for naturalization purposes?
questions.answer: The sources present conflicting interpretations regarding whether a notice to appear is the same as a warrant of arrest for naturalization purposes. The Ninth Circuit has concluded that a "warrant of arrest" and a "notice to appear" are distinct documents, noting that a notice to appear is akin to a summons and does not direct law enforcement to arrest an individual [S1][S2][S4]. Conversely, the government relies on 8 C.F.R. § 318.1, which states that for the purposes of 8 U.S.C. § 1429, a notice to appear "shall be regarded as a warrant of arrest" [S3]. The Seventh Circuit has upheld this interpretation, reasoning that an agency may define its own vocabulary to treat a notice to appear as a warrant of arrest [S5].

questions.question: Can I sue under the Administrative Procedure Act instead of the naturalization review statute?
questions.answer: The Administrative Procedure Act (APA) is not a statute that confers jurisdiction [S5]. APA lawsuits are subject to statutes that preclude judicial review, including exhaustion requirements, and there is no general exception to these requirements for constitutional claims when a statute expressly provides for judicial review [S1]. Furthermore, 8 U.S.C. § 1421(c) specifically mandates that judicial review of naturalization denials be conducted in accordance with the APA [S5].

questions.question: Do I have to go to the USCIS hearing before I can take my denial to court?
questions.answer:
Whether you must attend a USCIS hearing before going to court depends on the circumstances of your case:

*   **If USCIS fails to make a determination:** If USCIS does not make a determination on your initial application within 120 days of your examination, you may apply to a district court for a hearing on the matter without first attending an administrative hearing [S2][S3].
*   **If your application was denied:** If your application was denied, you must exhaust administrative remedies—which includes requesting and attending a hearing before an immigration officer—before you can seek judicial review of that denial in a district court [S5].

questions.question: Does something I did before I applied count against my good moral character?
questions.answer: Yes, conduct that occurred before the five-year statutory period preceding your application can be considered when determining your good moral character [S2][S5]. The Attorney General is not limited to the five years preceding the filing of an application and may consider conduct at any time prior to that period to determine if an applicant has reformed [S2][S5]. Additionally, certain acts, such as a conviction for an aggravated felony, can bar a finding of good moral character regardless of when they occurred [S4].
